Beyond Logit Adjustment: A Residual Decomposition Framework for Long-Tailed Reranking

Zhanliang Wang Affiliation:  University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA Affiliation:  Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, Philadelphia, PA, USA    Hongzhuo Chen Affiliation:  University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA Affiliation:  Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, Philadelphia, PA, USA    Quan Minh Nguyen Affiliation:  University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA Affiliation:  Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, Philadelphia, PA, USA    Mian Umair Ahsan,   Kai Wang ††thanks: Corresponding author. Email: wangk@chop.edu Affiliation:  University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA Affiliation:  Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, Philadelphia, PA, USA
Abstract

Long-tailed classification, where a small number of frequent classes dominate many rare ones, remains challenging because models systematically favor frequent classes at inference time. Existing post-hoc methods such as logit adjustment address this by adding a fixed classwise offset to the base-model logits. However, the correction required to restore the relative ranking of two classes need not be constant across inputs, and a fixed offset cannot adapt to such variation. We study this problem through Bayes-optimal reranking on a base-model top-kk shortlist. The gap between the optimal score and the base score, the residual correction, decomposes into a classwise component that is constant within each class, and a pairwise component that depends on the input and competing labels. When the residual is purely classwise, a fixed offset suffices to recover the Bayes-optimal ordering. We further show that when the same label pair induces incompatible ordering constraints across contexts, no fixed offset can achieve this recovery. This decomposition leads to testable predictions regarding when pairwise correction can improve performance and when cannot. We develop Repair (Reranking via Pairwise residual correction), a lightweight post-hoc reranker that combines a shrinkage-stabilized classwise term with a linear pairwise term driven by competition features on the shortlist. Experiments on five benchmarks spanning image classification, species recognition, scene recognition, and rare disease diagnosis confirm that the decomposition explains where pairwise correction helps and where classwise correction alone suffices.

Code: https://github.com/WGLab/REPAIR

1 Introduction

Long-tailed classification, where a few common classes dominate many rare ones, remains a persistent challenge because models systematically favor frequent classes at prediction time, pushing rare labels down the ranking even when they are plausible. A common post-hoc correction method is logit adjustment (Menon et al., 2021), which adds a fixed class-dependent offset to the base-model scores. This is effective when rare classes are globally under-ranked due to bias introduced by training frequency, but long-tailed ranking errors are more complicated than a single classwise offset can express.

Consider an animal classifier trained on far more images of cat than leopard (Figure 1). On a clear photograph showing a leopard’s rosette pattern, the model assigns 56%56\% to cat and 44%44\% to leopard. On a distant, partially occluded shot of a leopard, the model gives 70%70\% to cat and only 30%30\%to leopard. On a third image that genuinely depicts a cat, the model gives 67%67\% to cat and 33%33\% to leopard. No single fixed per-class offset works for all three: a value small enough to preserve the correct ranking on the third image cannot close the gap on the second, while a value large enough to correct the second inevitably flips the third. The root cause is data imbalance: with few training images of leopard, the base model’s scores for this class are not only biased but highly variable across inputs, and this variability is exactly what a fixed offset cannot absorb.

We formalize this by studying Bayes-optimal reranking on a base-model shortlist. The gap between the optimal score and the base score, the residual correction, decomposes into a classwise component, which depends only on the label identity; and a pairwise component, which varies with the input and the competing labels; Section 4 characterizes precisely when the classwise component alone suffices and when it does not. Real datasets fall on a spectrum between these extremes, and the degree of pairwise competition determines how much a context-dependent correction can help. This raises a practical question: how should a reranker adapt its correction to the specific input and the competing labels on the shortlist? Our key insight is that the competition structure within the shortlist already encodes this information: how closely the base model scores the true label relative to each rival reflects how hard the current input is, and this relative strength varies across inputs, which is exactly the variation that a fixed offset misses.

Based on this analysis, we develop Repair (Reranking via Pairwise residual correction), a lightweight post-hoc reranker that combines a shrinkage-stabilized classwise term, which alone improves over logit adjustment by learning offsets on the shortlist, with a linear pairwise term driven by competition features. Both components are fitted jointly on covered held-out calibration examples; the base model is never modified. We validate on five long-tailed benchmarks, with small gains on vision benchmarks (ImageNet-LT (Liu et al., 2019), Places-LT (Liu et al., 2019), iNaturalist (Van Horn et al., 2018)) and substantially larger gains on rare-disease diagnosis (GestaltMatcher Database (GMDB) (Lesmann et al., 2024)) and an out-of-distribution variant (RareBench (Chen et al., 2024)). The decomposition framework explains this contrast: gains arise where the classwise correction is insufficient and vanish where it suffices.

Contributions.
  1. 1.

    We decompose the residual correction on a fixed shortlist into classwise and pairwise components, proving that when the same label pair induces incompatible ordering constraints across inputs, no fixed per-class offset can recover the Bayes ordering (Theorem 4.3).

  2. 2.

    We derive Repair, a lightweight post-hoc reranker from this decomposition, combining a learned classwise correction with a linear pairwise term.

  3. 3.

    We validate the framework’s predictions on five benchmarks: gains are proportional to the degree of pairwise competition and concentrated where the theory predicts fixed offsets to be the most fragile.

2 Related Work

Long-tailed distribution.

Real world class distributions are rarely uniform. Typically a few head classes dominate many rare ones, forming a long-tailed distribution (Yang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023). Models trained on such datasets are systematically biased towards frequent classes, which usually results in poor performance on the tail (Ren et al., 2020; Menon et al., 2021). Existing solutions can be grouped into two main categories based on when the correction is applied: training-time methods and post-hoc methods.

Post-hoc score correction.

Post-hoc methods adjust the output of a fixed pretrained model at inference time. Logit adjustment methods add a fixed per-class offset to correct the distribution shift (Ren et al., 2020; Menon et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2021). Weight normalization methods rescale the classifier weight norms to remove the correlation between norm magnitude and class frequency (Kang et al., 2020; Kim and Kim, 2020). The correction for each class remains fixed, which is a common limitation shared by all these methods. Temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2025) is also post-hoc but rank-preserving, targeting calibration rather than ordering. A broader review of training-time methods is provided in Appendix A.

Rare-disease diagnosis.

Many rare genetic disorders present distinctive facial features, and CNN-based systems (Gurovich et al., 2019; Hsieh et al., 2022) can prioritize candidate diagnoses from facial photos across hundreds of syndromes. Recent multimodal approaches further integrate clinical notes and demographic information via large language models (Wu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026), yet the extreme class imbalance inherent in rare disease settings remains a core challenge across all these systems.

3 Preliminaries

We consider a multiclass classification problem with input XX, label Y∈[K]={1,…,K}Y\in[K]=\{1,\dots,K\}, and long-tailed class prior πy=P⁡(Y=y)\pi_{y}=P(Y=y). A trained base model produces scores g⁡(X)=(g1​(X),…,gK​(X))∈ℝKg(X)=(g_{1}(X),\dots,g_{K}(X))\in\mathbb{R}^{K}.

Shortlist and coverage.

Fix an integer k≪Kk\ll K and let S⁡(X)⊆[K]S(X)\subseteq[K] denote the deterministic top-kk shortlist under g⁡(X)g(X), with deterministic tie-breaking. A reranker selects a label y^​(X)∈S​(X)\hat{y}(X)\in S(X). Write C:={Y∈S(X)}C:=\{Y\in S(X)\} for the coverage event; every reranker satisfies P⁡(y^​(X)=Y)≤P⁡(C)=Recall@​kP(\hat{y}(X)=Y)\leq P(C)=\text{Recall@}k, so shortlist recall is a hard ceiling on reranking accuracy. Since reranking can only affect covered examples, we condition all subsequent analysis and evaluation metrics on CC.

Shortlist posterior.

Once the shortlist is fixed, the relevant object for reranking is the posterior restricted to the shortlisted labels:

pS​(y∣x):=P⁡(Y=y∣X=x,C),y∈S.p_{S}(y\mid x):=P(Y=y\mid X=x,\,C),\qquad y\in S. (1)

The corresponding log-posterior,

sy⋆​(x,S):=log⁡pS​(y∣x),s^{\star}_{y}(x,S):=\log p_{S}(y\mid x), (2)

is the Bayes-optimal shortlist score: a standard pointwise argument (Appendix C.4.1) shows that the Bayes-optimal reranker selects y^⋆​(x)∈arg⁡maxy∈S⁡(x)​pS​(y∣x)\hat{y}^{\star}(x)\in\arg\max_{y\in S(x)}p_{S}(y\mid x). Throughout, only relative values of sy⋆s^{\star}_{y} across y∈Sy\in S matter for ranking. A generic classwise reranker modifies the base score as gy​(x)+ayg_{y}(x)+a_{y} for a fixed per-class offset aya_{y}; prior-based logit adjustment is the special choice ay=−τ​log⁡πya_{y}=-\tau\log\pi_{y}. The next section discusses when this classwise form is sufficient and when it is not.

4 A Residual Correction Framework for Long-Tailed Reranking

Once a base model returns a fixed shortlist, the first question is what score a Bayes-optimal reranker should target. The second is how the base score differs from this target. That gap defines a residual correction. We then ask when this correction can be represented by a fixed classwise term, and when context-dependent competition makes a pairwise term necessary.

4.1 Residual correction and pairwise gaps

For each shortlisted label y∈Sy\in S, define the residual correction

βy⋆​(x,S):=sy⋆​(x,S)−gy​(x).\beta^{\star}_{y}(x,S)\;:=\;s^{\star}_{y}(x,S)\;-\;g_{y}(x). (3)

Because ranking depends only on score differences, the relevant object is the pairwise gap

Δu​v​(x,S):=βu⋆​(x,S)−βv⋆​(x,S)=(su⋆−sv⋆)−(gu​(x)−gv​(x)),u,v∈S.\Delta_{uv}(x,S)\;:=\;\beta^{\star}_{u}(x,S)-\beta^{\star}_{v}(x,S)\;=\;\bigl(s^{\star}_{u}-s^{\star}_{v}\bigr)-\bigl(g_{u}(x)-g_{v}(x)\bigr),\qquad u,v\in S. (4)

The quantity Δu​v​(x,S)\Delta_{uv}(x,S) is invariant to any shortlist-shared additive constant in β⋆\beta^{\star} and captures exactly the correction difference needed to recover the Bayes ordering of the pair (u,v)(u,v).

Definition 4.1 (Class-separable and non-class-separable regimes).

The setting is class-separable if there exists a vector a∈ℝKa\in\mathbb{R}^{K} such that for every covered (x,S)(x,S) and every u,v∈Su,v\in S,

Δu​v​(x,S)=au−av.\Delta_{uv}(x,S)=a_{u}-a_{v}. (5)

Equivalently, there exists a shortlist-shared scalar c⁡(x,S)c(x,S) such that βy⋆​(x,S)=ay+c⁡(x,S)\beta^{\star}_{y}(x,S)=a_{y}+c(x,S) for all y∈Sy\in S. If no such vector aa exists, the setting is non-class-separable.

Intuitively, class-separable means that the ranking bias of each class can be summarized by a single number. Prior-based logit adjustment assumes exactly this structure: the correction depends only on the training frequency of the class, not on which rivals appear or how the input looks.

Proposition 4.2 (Classwise correction as an exact special case).

If the setting is class-separable, then the fixed-offset score ry​(x,S)=gy​(x)+ayr_{y}(x,S)=g_{y}(x)+a_{y} induces the Bayes-optimal ordering on every covered example.

This positions logit adjustment precisely: it is exact when the residual correction is class-separable up to a shortlist-shared constant. Proof in Appendix C.4.3. The next subsection shows why this condition fails in general.

4.2 Why a pairwise correction is necessary

For classes u,v∈[K]u,v\in[K], define the base-score threshold

t⁡(x,u,v):=gv​(x)−gu​(x).t(x;\,u,v)\;:=\;g_{v}(x)-g_{u}(x). (6)

A fixed classwise model ranks uu above vv if and only if au−av>t⁡(x,u,v)a_{u}-a_{v}>t(x;\,u,v). Thus a single cut au−ava_{u}-a_{v} must satisfy the requirements of all contexts in which the pair (u,v)(u,v) appears.

Theorem 4.3 (Necessity of pairwise correction).

Suppose there exist two covered contexts (x,S)(x,S) and (x′,S′)(x^{\prime},S^{\prime}) and two labels u,v∈S∩S′u,v\in S\cap S^{\prime} such that the Bayes rule ranks uu above vv at xx, ranks vv above uu at x′x^{\prime}, and

t⁡(x,u,v)≥t⁡(x′,u,v).t(x;\,u,v)\;\geq\;t(x^{\prime};\,u,v). (7)

Then no fixed offset vector a∈ℝKa\in\mathbb{R}^{K} can agree with the Bayes ordering in both contexts.

Theorem 4.3 identifies the precise point at which fixed classwise correction breaks down. Input-dependent pairwise variation alone does not force failure; the critical event is a threshold crossing for the same pair across contexts. We call such a pair contradictory. A setting may be non-class-separable without containing a contradictory pair, but once such a pair appears, no fixed classwise offset can agree with the Bayes ordering in all relevant contexts. In practice, a dataset can have large per-class score variance yet still be fully correctable by a fixed offset, as long as the variation does not reverse the ordering of any pair. Proof in Appendix C.4.4.

Threshold dispersion.

Theorem 4.3 shows that threshold crossings drive the failure of fixed offsets. To quantify how prone a class is to such crossings, we define

Dy​(S):=maxj∈S∖{y}⁡std⁡(t⁡(x,y,j)),D_{y}(S)\;:=\;\max_{j\in S\setminus\{y\}}\mathrm{std}\bigl(t(x;\,y,j)\bigr), (8)

where the standard deviation is computed across all covered contexts in which both yy and jj appear in the shortlist. Large DyD_{y} means the true label faces at least one rival whose score gap fluctuates widely across inputs: some inputs are easy to distinguish, others are not, and no single fixed offset can handle both. In Section 6, we compute the mean threshold dispersion per rare class across all its covered test examples, then sort rare classes into five equal-sized quintiles (Q1–Q5, lowest to highest; we call these contradiction quintiles since high DyD_{y} is a necessary condition for threshold crossings) and show that the gain of Repair over classwise-only increases from Q1 to Q5.

4.3 Measuring reranking gains

Since all evaluation is conditioned on coverage, we normalize reranking gains by the recoverable gap within the shortlist:

ρk​(y^):=Hit​@​1​(y^)−Hit​@​1​(y^base)1−Hit​@​1​(y^base),\rho_{k}(\hat{y})\;:=\;\frac{\mathrm{Hit@1}(\hat{y})\;-\;\mathrm{Hit@1}(\hat{y}_{\mathrm{base}})}{1\;-\;\mathrm{Hit@1}(\hat{y}_{\mathrm{base}})}, (9)

where Hit​@​1​(y^):=P⁡(y^​(X)=Y∣C)\mathrm{Hit@1}(\hat{y}):=P(\hat{y}(X)=Y\mid C). The denominator is the fraction of covered examples the base model fails to rank first; ρk=1\rho_{k}=1 means the reranker corrects all such failures. We use ρk\rho_{k} primarily in the synthetic validation below; for real-data experiments, we report Hit@1 and HFR directly since they are more interpretable across datasets with different coverage rates. The equivalent unconditional form is given in Appendix C.3.

4.4 Synthetic validation

To verify the predictions of Proposition 4.2 and Theorem 4.3, we construct two controlled settings: one where the residual is class-separable, and one where confuser pairs induce threshold crossings (setup in Appendix F.1). Figure 2 confirms both predictions: in the class-separable setting, classwise reranking and REPAIR achieve the same ρk\rho_{k} (=0.17=0.17); in the non-class-separable setting with contradictory pairs, REPAIR closes substantially more of the recoverable gap (ρk=0.42\rho_{k}=0.42 vs. 0.180.18).

5 Algorithm

Theorem 4.3 identifies the missing degree of freedom: the correction for a label cannot depend only on the label identity; it must also vary with the competing labels on the shortlist. More precisely, the excess risk of any plug-in reranker is controlled by how well it estimates the shortlist posterior (Appendix C.4.2), which in turn depends on approximating both the classwise and pairwise components of the residual. This section translates that structural insight into a concrete, lightweight algorithm.

5.1 Score model

We model the reranker score as

ry​(x,S)=gy​(x)+ay⏟classwise+ℓy​(x,S)⏟pairwise,y∈S,r_{y}(x,S)\;=\;g_{y}(x)\;+\;\underbrace{a_{y}}_{\text{classwise}}\;+\;\underbrace{\ell_{y}(x,S)}_{\text{pairwise}},\qquad y\in S, (10)

where β^y:=ay+ℓy​(x,S)\hat{\beta}_{y}:=a_{y}+\ell_{y}(x,S) is our estimate of the residual correction βy⋆\beta^{\star}_{y} (Eq. 3). The classwise term aya_{y} targets the class-separable component of βy⋆\beta^{\star}_{y} (Definition 4.1); the special choice ay=−τ​log⁡πya_{y}=-\tau\log\pi_{y} recovers logit adjustment, but we learn aya_{y} from covered calibration examples to obtain the strongest fixed-classwise correction. Even without pairwise term, this learned classwise correction outperforms the closed-form logit adjustment offset on most datasets (Table 1), because it captures per-class biases beyond frequency. The pairwise term ℓy\ell_{y} targets the remainder that fixed classwise corrections structurally miss (Theorem 4.3).

The pairwise correction averages over all rivals in the shortlist:

ℓy​(x,S)=1|S|−1​∑j∈S∖{y}θ⊤​ϕ​(x,y,j).\ell_{y}(x,S)\;=\;\frac{1}{|S|-1}\sum_{j\in S\setminus\{y\}}\theta^{\top}\phi(x,y,j). (11)

Each shortlisted rival jj contributes a correction to label yy through the shared parameter vector θ\theta and the pairwise feature vector ϕ⁡(x,y,j)\phi(x,y,j).

5.2 Pairwise features

The feature vector ϕ⁡(x,y,j)\phi(x,y,j) encodes how label yy competes against rival jj in context xx. Four competition features are computed from the base model’s output: the score gap gy​(x)−gj​(x)g_{y}(x)-g_{j}(x) (the negative of the threshold t⁡(x,y,j)t(x;\,y,j) in Eq. 6), the rank gap rank⁡(j)−rank⁡(y)\mathrm{rank}(j)-\mathrm{rank}(y), the log-frequency ratio log⁡ny−log⁡nj\log n_{y}-\log n_{j}, where nyn_{y} denotes the number of training examples for class yy, and the log-probability ratio log⁡P⁡(y|S)/P⁡(j|S)\log P(y|S)/P(j|S). Label-similarity features encode how confusable two classes are: taxonomic distance for iNaturalist, WordNet path similarity for ImageNet-LT, and HPO phenotype similarity for the rare-disease benchmarks (Appendix D.2).

5.3 Training and shrinkage

All parameters are estimated on covered examples from a held-out calibration set with (yi∈Siy_{i}\in S_{i}). The base model is never modified. We fit aa and θ\theta jointly by maximizing a conditional multinomial logit on the shortlist:

qθ,a​(y∣x,S)=exp⁡(ry​(x,S))∑j∈Sexp⁡(rj​(x,S)),y∈S.q_{\theta,a}(y\mid x,S)\;=\;\frac{\exp\bigl(r_{y}(x,S)\bigr)}{\sum_{j\in S}\exp\bigl(r_{j}(x,S)\bigr)},\quad y\in S. (12)

The training objective is the regularized conditional log-likelihood:

ℒ⁡(a,θ,𝒟)=∑(xi,Si,yi)∈𝒟log⁡qθ,a​(yi∣xi,Si)−λθ​‖θ‖22−λa​‖a‖22,\mathcal{L}(a,\theta;\,\mathcal{D})\;=\;\sum_{(x_{i},S_{i},y_{i})\in\mathcal{D}}\log q_{\theta,a}(y_{i}\mid x_{i},S_{i})\;-\;\lambda_{\theta}\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}\;-\;\lambda_{a}\|a\|_{2}^{2}, (13)

where 𝒟={(xi,Si,yi):yi∈Si}\mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},S_{i},y_{i}):y_{i}\in S_{i}\} is the set of covered examples.

Shrinkage.

For rare classes with very few covered examples, aya_{y} can be noisy. We stabilize via empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward a frequency-group mean:

ay⋆←(1−λy)​a^y+λy​μb⁡(y),λy=σy2σy2+νb⁡(y)2,a^{\star}_{y}\leftarrow(1-\lambda_{y})\,\hat{a}_{y}+\lambda_{y}\,\mu_{b(y)},\qquad\lambda_{y}=\frac{\sigma^{2}_{y}}{\sigma^{2}_{y}+\nu^{2}_{b(y)}}, (14)

where b⁡(y)b(y) indexes a frequency group, μb⁡(y)\mu_{b(y)} is the group mean, and σy2\sigma^{2}_{y}, νb⁡(y)2\nu^{2}_{b(y)} are within-class and between-group variance estimates (Appendix C.4.7). The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1 (Appendix D.1).

6 Experiments

6.1 Setup

Datasets and base models.

We evaluate on five benchmarks spanning image classification (ImageNet-LT, 1,000 classes; Places-LT, 365 classes), species recognition (iNaturalist 2018, 8,142 classes), and rare-disease diagnosis (GMDB, 508 classes; RareBench, 508 classes, out-of-distribution). Base models range from ResNet-50/152 with cRT classifiers to a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B; full details are in Appendix E.1. In all cases, REPAIR operates on a fixed top-kk shortlist (k=10k{=}10) produced by the base model; the base model is never modified. We designate the bottom 80% of classes by training-set frequency as rare and the top 20% as frequent.

Baselines.

All methods share the same shortlist. Base ranks by the raw scores gy​(x)g_{y}(x). LogitAdj (Menon et al., 2021) adds −τ​log⁡πy-\tau\log\pi_{y} with τ\tau tuned on the calibration set. τ\tau-norm (Kang et al., 2020) divides by the classifier weight norm ‖wy‖τ\|w_{y}\|^{\tau}. Classwise learns per-class offsets aya_{y} via Eq. 13 with shrinkage (Eq. 14), setting θ=0\theta=0. REPAIR adds the pairwise term ℓy​(x,S)\ell_{y}(x,S).

Evaluation schemes.

Reranker parameters are estimated on a held-out calibration set and evaluated on an independent test set; the two never overlap. Each experiment is repeated over five trials, each subsampling 80%80\% of the calibration set with a distinct seed. We report mean ±\pm std for methods with learned parameters (Classwise, REPAIR) and single values for LogitAdj and τ\tau-norm, whose corrections are deterministic given the training-set frequency distribution and a fixed τ\tau (tuned once on the full calibration set), and therefore do not vary across calibration subsamples. Significance is assessed via a sign test (≥4/5\geq 4/5 wins); full results are in Appendix F.7. All metrics are conditioned on coverage (Y∈SY\in S). We report Hit@1, Hit@3, MRR, Rare Hit@1, Frequent Hit@1, and the hardest-rival flip rate (HFR; Definition 6.1), which measures whether the reranker can beat the strongest wrong competitor on inputs the base model misranks.

Definition 6.1 (Hardest-rival flip rate).

The probability that the reranker ranks the true label above the base model’s top-scoring wrong class, among covered examples the base model misranks:

HFR⁡(y^)=P⁡(rY>rh⁡(X,Y)∣C,y^base≠Y),\mathrm{HFR}(\hat{y})=P\bigl(r_{Y}>r_{h(X,Y)}\mid C,\;\hat{y}_{\mathrm{base}}\neq Y\bigr),

where h⁡(x,y):=arg⁡maxj∈S⁡(x)∖{y}​gj​(x)h(x,y):=\arg\max_{j\in S(x)\setminus\{y\}}g_{j}(x).

6.2 Results

Table 1 reports the full comparison. The decomposition makes a direct prediction: on datasets where the base model’s score gaps are stable across inputs, classwise correction should suffice and the pairwise term should add little; on datasets where score gaps vary widely, the pairwise term should provide substantial gains.

Near-class-separable regime (vision benchmarks).

On iNaturalist, ImageNet-LT, and Places-LT, REPAIR provides small but consistent Hit@1 improvements over Classwise (+0.2%+0.2\%, +0.2%+0.2\%, +0.4%+0.4\%), with the learned Classwise correction competitive with or outperforming LogitAdj on all three. HFR nearly doubles on iNaturalist (0.074→0.1380.074\to 0.138) and ImageNet-LT (0.336→0.3780.336\to 0.378). On Places-LT, LogitAdj and τ\tau-norm both degrade Hit@1 relative to Base, while Classwise and REPAIR both exceed it, confirming that learned offsets are more robust than closed-form corrections. The decomposition identifies these datasets as predominantly classwise: most ranking errors are correctable by a fixed per-class offset.

Non-class-separable regime (rare-disease benchmarks).

On GMDB, REPAIR improves Hit@1 from 71.471.4 to 72.372.3 and HFR from 0.4410.441 to 0.5100.510. On RareBench (OOD), Hit@1 rises from 66.266.2 to 85.685.6 (+19.4+19.4 %) and HFR from 0.2150.215 to 0.7080.708. Two factors drive this: the base model operates out-of-distribution (trained on GMDB with image and text, tested on text), which amplifies threshold variation across inputs; and HPO phenotype similarity gives the pairwise term discriminative signal the base model has no access to. The RareBench test set contains only 32 covered examples, so we verify this result with 10K-resample bootstrap: the 95% CI for the gain over Classwise is [+6.2,+31.2](%)[+6.2,\;+31.2](\%)(P=0.999P{=}0.999; Appendix F.8).

Head–tail trade-off.

On vision benchmarks, improving Rare Hit@1 comes at some cost to Frequent Hit@1. Most of this shift originates from the classwise correction itself; the pairwise term adds only a small further change. On RareBench, both strata improve simultaneously.

Component ablation.

In the synthetic setting (Figure 6, Appendix F.3), CW-only matches REPAIR in the class-separable regime while PW-only adds nothing; in the non-class-separable regime, the full model outperforms both (72.572.5 vs. 61.161.1 CW-only, 72.172.1 PW-only). On real data (Appendix F.3), the relative importance of the two components shifts across the spectrum. On iNaturalist, PW-only alone matches REPAIR (Rare Hit@1: 42.142.1), suggesting that the pairwise features implicitly absorb the classwise correction. On ImageNet-LT, Places-LT and GMDB, both components contribute incrementally. On RareBench, neither component alone approaches the full model (CW-only 58.858.8, PW-only 47.147.1, REPAIR 88.288.2; single random seed): the classwise term calibrates the score scale while the pairwise term redirects rankings, and joint estimation is essential for the two corrections to reinforce each other.

6.3 Quintile analysis

We stratify rare classes by their mean threshold dispersion DyD_{y} (Eq. 8) into five equal-sized quintiles and measure the Δ\DeltaHit@1 of REPAIR over Classwise within each bin. In the class-separable setting (a), the gain is uniformly small and flat, which means DyD_{y} does not modulate the pairwise contribution when the residual is approximately classwise. In the non-class-separable setting (b), the gain increases monotonically from Q1 (+6%+6\%) to Q5 (+30%+30\%). On real data (Appendix F.4), the same pattern holds: on GMDB, Q5 shows the largest gain while Q1 shows the smallest, consistent with the non-class-separable regime; on iNaturalist, the gain is uniformly small and the quintile gradient is flat, consistent with a near-class-separable residual. ImageNet-LT and Places-LT fall between these extremes.

7 Conclusion

In this work, we proposed a residual decomposition framework for post-hoc reranking under long-tailed class distributions. Unlike logit adjustment, which applies a fixed per-class offset derived from class frequencies, our framework decomposes the Bayes-optimal correction into a learned classwise term and an input-dependent pairwise term, with a formal characterization of when the classwise component alone is sufficient and when it is not. Empirically, the learned classwise correction already outperforms logit adjustment on most datasets, and the pairwise term provides further gains proportional to the degree of threshold variation across five benchmarks spanning vision and rare-disease diagnosis, with especially large improvements in the rare-disease setting where phenotypically similar conditions create strong pairwise competition. The current pairwise features are compact and domain-interpretable, but richer representations learned from the base model’s embeddings could capture competition patterns that hand-crafted features miss. Overall, these results demonstrate that in long-tailed settings, decomposing the residual correction into classwise and pairwise components offers a principled and lightweight alternative to purely frequency-based post-hoc adjustments, particularly in domains where local competition between similar classes causes ranking errors that no fixed offset can resolve.

Ethics Statement

This work applies post-hoc reranking to rare-disease diagnosis, a high-stakes clinical setting. REPAIR is designed as a decision-support tool that reorders a candidate shortlist; it does not make final diagnostic decisions. This study is approved by the institutional review board at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP). All datasets used in this work are publicly available.

Use of Generative AI

We used large language models (Claude Opus 4.6) to polish grammar and improve the clarity of our writing, to organize the structure and logical flow of the paper, and to check and refine the presentation of mathematical proofs. All scientific contributions, experimental design, and final content were produced and verified by the authors.

Appendix A Additional Related Work

Training-time corrections.

Training time methods modify the loss, sampling or architecture during learning. Re-weighing approaches adjust per-class loss contributions based on class frequency or sample difficulties  (Lin et al., 2020; Cui et al., 2019), while margin-based methods enforce larger-decision margin for rare classes (Cao et al., 2019). At sampling level, decoupled training learns representation with standard sampling and re-balances the classifier (Kang et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2021). Ensemble methods in addition offer structural solution by training multiple experts with complementary skills across frequent classes (Zhang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).

Appendix C Theoretical Supplement

C.1 Restricted posterior on the shortlist

Because S⁡(x)S(x) is a deterministic function of xx, the coverage probability given X=xX=x is

α⁡(x):=P⁡(C∣X=x)=∑j∈S⁡(x)P⁡(Y=j∣X=x).\alpha(x):=P(C\mid X=x)=\sum_{j\in S(x)}P(Y=j\mid X=x). (15)

Whenever α⁡(x)>0\alpha(x)>0,

pS​(y∣x)=P⁡(Y=y∣X=x,C)=P(Y=y∣X=x)⋅𝟏{y∈S(x)}α⁡(x).p_{S}(y\mid x)=P(Y=y\mid X=x,C)=\frac{P(Y=y\mid X=x)\cdot\mathbf{1}\{y\in S(x)\}}{\alpha(x)}. (16)

Hence the Bayes-optimal shortlist score is

sy⋆​(x,S)=log⁡pS​(y∣x)=log⁡P⁡(Y=y∣X=x)−log⁡α⁡(x),y∈S⁡(x),s^{\star}_{y}(x,S)=\log p_{S}(y\mid x)=\log P(Y=y\mid X=x)-\log\alpha(x),\qquad y\in S(x), (17)

so only the relative values across y∈S⁡(x)y\in S(x) matter for ranking. The term log⁡α⁡(x)\log\alpha(x) is shared by all labels in the shortlist and therefore cancels out of any pairwise comparison.

C.2 Weighted variant

The paper uses ordinary top-1 risk for clarity. If one instead optimizes a class-weighted risk with weights wy>0w_{y}>0, then the Bayes-optimal shortlist score becomes log⁡wy+log⁡pS​(y∣x)\log w_{y}+\log p_{S}(y\mid x). All main arguments carry over verbatim after adding log⁡wy\log w_{y} to the ideal score. We keep the unweighted version in the main text because it is easier to read.

C.3 Unconditional form of the recoverable gap closure

When expressed in unconditional accuracy, the recoverable gap closure (9) takes the equivalent form

ρk​(y^)=Acc⁡(y^)−Acc⁡(y^base)P⁡(C)−Acc⁡(y^base),\rho_{k}(\hat{y})=\frac{\mathrm{Acc}(\hat{y})-\mathrm{Acc}(\hat{y}_{\mathrm{base}})}{P(C)-\mathrm{Acc}(\hat{y}_{\mathrm{base}})}, (18)

since Hit​@​1​(y^)=Acc⁡(y^)/P⁡(C)\mathrm{Hit@1}(\hat{y})=\mathrm{Acc}(\hat{y})/P(C) and the P⁡(C)P(C) factors cancel. This equivalence holds because all rerankers share the same shortlist and hence the same coverage P⁡(C)P(C).

C.4 Proofs

C.4.1 Bayes-optimal reranking on the shortlist

Proposition C.1 (Bayes rule on a fixed shortlist).

Among all measurable rules y^​(X)∈S​(X)\hat{y}(X)\in S(X), a Bayes-optimal reranker can be chosen pointwise as y^⋆​(x)∈arg⁡maxy∈S⁡(x)​pS​(y∣x)\hat{y}^{\star}(x)\in\arg\max_{y\in S(x)}p_{S}(y\mid x). Equivalently, any score function strictly increasing in pS​(y∣x)p_{S}(y\mid x) yields the same Bayes ordering.

Proof.

Fix xx. Among all measurable rules r⁡(x)∈S⁡(x)r(x)\in S(x), the conditional probability of being correct is

P(r(X)=Y∣X=x,C)=∑y∈S⁡(x)𝟏{r(x)=y}pS(y∣x)=pS(r(x)∣x).P(r(X)=Y\mid X=x,C)=\sum_{y\in S(x)}\mathbf{1}\{r(x)=y\}\,p_{S}(y\mid x)=p_{S}(r(x)\mid x).

Since r⁡(x)r(x) is a deterministic choice, the indicator is nonzero for exactly one value of yy, and the sum collapses to pS​(r​(x)∣x)p_{S}(r(x)\mid x). Therefore the conditional risk given X=xX=x and CC is minimized by any r⁡(x)∈arg⁡maxy∈S⁡(x)​pS​(y∣x)r(x)\in\arg\max_{y\in S(x)}p_{S}(y\mid x). Since this argument is pointwise in xx, any measurable selector of that argmax is Bayes-optimal on covered examples. ∎

C.4.2 Plug-in estimation error

Proposition C.2 (Plug-in control).

Let p^S(⋅∣x)\hat{p}_{S}(\cdot\mid x) be an estimate of pS(⋅∣x)p_{S}(\cdot\mid x), and let y^plug​(x)∈arg⁡maxy∈S⁡(x)​p^S​(y∣x)\hat{y}_{\mathrm{plug}}(x)\in\arg\max_{y\in S(x)}\hat{p}_{S}(y\mid x). Then the conditional excess risk on covered examples satisfies

P(y^plug(X)≠Y∣C)−P(y^⋆(X)≠Y∣C)≤2𝔼[∥p^S(⋅∣x)−pS(⋅∣x)∥1∣C].P(\hat{y}_{\mathrm{plug}}(X)\neq Y\mid C)-P(\hat{y}^{\star}(X)\neq Y\mid C)\leq 2\,\mathbb{E}[\|\hat{p}_{S}(\cdot\mid x)-p_{S}(\cdot\mid x)\|_{1}\mid C]. (19)
Lemma C.3 (Covered excess-risk identity).

For any measurable shortlist rule y^​(X)∈S​(X)\hat{y}(X)\in S(X),

P⁡(y^​(X)≠Y∣C)−P⁡(y^⋆​(X)≠Y∣C)=𝔼⁡[pS​(y^⋆​(X)∣x)−pS​(y^​(X)∣x)∣C].P(\hat{y}(X)\neq Y\mid C)-P(\hat{y}^{\star}(X)\neq Y\mid C)=\mathbb{E}[p_{S}(\hat{y}^{\star}(X)\mid x)-p_{S}(\hat{y}(X)\mid x)\mid C].
Proof.

Condition on X=xX=x and CC. The conditional error rates are 1−pS​(y^​(x)∣x)1-p_{S}(\hat{y}(x)\mid x) and 1−pS​(y^⋆​(x)∣x)1-p_{S}(\hat{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x), respectively. Subtracting:

(1−pS​(y^​(x)∣x))−(1−pS​(y^⋆​(x)∣x))=pS​(y^⋆​(x)∣x)−pS​(y^​(x)∣x).\bigl(1-p_{S}(\hat{y}(x)\mid x)\bigr)-\bigl(1-p_{S}(\hat{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)\bigr)=p_{S}(\hat{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)-p_{S}(\hat{y}(x)\mid x).

Taking expectations over XX given CC yields the identity. ∎

Proof of Proposition (Plug-in control).

Using the lemma,

Δ:=P⁡(y^plug​(X)≠Y∣C)−P⁡(y^⋆​(X)≠Y∣C)=𝔼⁡[pS​(y^⋆​(X)∣x)−pS​(y^plug​(X)∣x)∣C].\Delta:=P(\hat{y}_{\mathrm{plug}}(X)\neq Y\mid C)-P(\hat{y}^{\star}(X)\neq Y\mid C)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[p_{S}(\hat{y}^{\star}(X)\mid x)-p_{S}(\hat{y}_{\mathrm{plug}}(X)\mid x)\mid C\bigr].

For each xx, we add and subtract p^S\hat{p}_{S}:

pS​(y^⋆​(x)∣x)−pS​(y^plug​(x)∣x)\displaystyle p_{S}(\hat{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)-p_{S}(\hat{y}_{\mathrm{plug}}(x)\mid x) =pS​(y^⋆​(x)∣x)−p^S​(y^⋆​(x)∣x)⏟(i)\displaystyle=\underbrace{p_{S}(\hat{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)-\hat{p}_{S}(\hat{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)}_{\text{(i)}}
+p^S​(y^⋆​(x)∣x)−p^S​(y^plug​(x)∣x)⏟(ii)\displaystyle\quad+\underbrace{\hat{p}_{S}(\hat{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)-\hat{p}_{S}(\hat{y}_{\mathrm{plug}}(x)\mid x)}_{\text{(ii)}}
+p^S​(y^plug​(x)∣x)−pS​(y^plug​(x)∣x)⏟(iii).\displaystyle\quad+\underbrace{\hat{p}_{S}(\hat{y}_{\mathrm{plug}}(x)\mid x)-p_{S}(\hat{y}_{\mathrm{plug}}(x)\mid x)}_{\text{(iii)}}.

Term (ii) ≤0\leq 0 by definition of y^plug\hat{y}_{\mathrm{plug}}. Each of terms (i) and (iii) is bounded by ∥p^S(⋅∣x)−pS(⋅∣x)∥1\|\hat{p}_{S}(\cdot\mid x)-p_{S}(\cdot\mid x)\|_{1}. Taking conditional expectations given CC completes the proof. ∎

C.4.3 Proof of Proposition 4.2

Proof.

If βy⋆​(x,S)=ay+c⁡(x,S)\beta^{\star}_{y}(x,S)=a_{y}+c(x,S) for every covered triple (x,S,y)(x,S,y) and some shortlist-shared scalar c⁡(x,S)c(x,S), then

sy⋆​(x,S)=gy​(x)+ay+c⁡(x,S)for all ​y∈S.s^{\star}_{y}(x,S)=g_{y}(x)+a_{y}+c(x,S)\quad\text{for all }y\in S.

Therefore the fixed-offset score gy​(x)+ayg_{y}(x)+a_{y} differs from the Bayes-optimal shortlist score only by the shortlist-shared constant c⁡(x,S)c(x,S). Since adding the same constant to all shortlisted labels does not change the ranking, the ordering induced by gy​(x)+ayg_{y}(x)+a_{y} is Bayes-optimal on every covered example. ∎

C.4.4 Proof of Theorem 4.3

Proof.

Assume for contradiction that some fixed-classwise model g⋅​(x)+a⋅g_{\cdot}(x)+a_{\cdot} agrees with the Bayes ordering in both contexts.

Because the Bayes rule ranks uu above vv at xx, the fixed-classwise model must satisfy gu​(x)+au>gv​(x)+avg_{u}(x)+a_{u}>g_{v}(x)+a_{v}, equivalently

au−av>gv​(x)−gu​(x)=t⁡(x,u,v).a_{u}-a_{v}>g_{v}(x)-g_{u}(x)=t(x;\,u,v). (20)

Because the Bayes rule ranks vv above uu at x′x^{\prime}, the same model must satisfy gv​(x′)+av>gu​(x′)+aug_{v}(x^{\prime})+a_{v}>g_{u}(x^{\prime})+a_{u}, equivalently

au−av<gv​(x′)−gu​(x′)=t⁡(x′,u,v).a_{u}-a_{v}<g_{v}(x^{\prime})-g_{u}(x^{\prime})=t(x^{\prime};\,u,v). (21)

Combining yields t⁡(x,u,v)<au−av<t⁡(x′,u,v)t(x;\,u,v)<a_{u}-a_{v}<t(x^{\prime};\,u,v), which requires t⁡(x,u,v)<t⁡(x′,u,v)t(x;\,u,v)<t(x^{\prime};\,u,v). But by assumption t⁡(x,u,v)≥t⁡(x′,u,v)t(x;\,u,v)\geq t(x^{\prime};\,u,v), a contradiction. ∎

C.4.5 Attainable frontier under fixed retrieval

Remark 1.

For any reranker y^​(X)∈S​(X)\hat{y}(X)\in S(X), the event {y^(X)=Y}\{\hat{y}(X)=Y\} implies CC, so P⁡(y^​(X)=Y)=P⁡(y^​(X)=Y,C)≤P⁡(C)P(\hat{y}(X)=Y)=P(\hat{y}(X)=Y,C)\leq P(C). Equivalently, Hit​@​1​(y^)≤1\mathrm{Hit@1}(\hat{y})\leq 1.

C.4.6 Conditional likelihood for the training objective

For covered training examples (xi,Si,yi)(x_{i},S_{i},y_{i}), the model

qθ,a​(y∣x,S)=exp⁡(ry​(x,S))∑j∈Sexp⁡(rj​(x,S))q_{\theta,a}(y\mid x,S)=\frac{\exp\bigl(r_{y}(x,S)\bigr)}{\sum_{j\in S}\exp\bigl(r_{j}(x,S)\bigr)}

is a standard multinomial logit model over the shortlist. Assuming conditional independence across covered examples, the log-likelihood is ∑i:yi∈Silogqθ,a(yi∣xi,Si)\sum_{i:\,y_{i}\in S_{i}}\log q_{\theta,a}(y_{i}\mid x_{i},S_{i}), and adding ℓ2\ell_{2} penalties yields Eq. (13).

C.4.7 Empirical-Bayes shrinkage

A simple way to stabilize rare-class offsets is to treat the raw estimate a~y\tilde{a}_{y} as a noisy observation of an unobserved true offset aya_{y}, and to place a Gaussian prior on aya_{y} within a frequency group b⁡(y)b(y):

a~y∣ay∼𝒩(ay,σy2),ay∼𝒩(μb⁡(y),νb⁡(y)2).\tilde{a}_{y}\mid a_{y}\sim\mathcal{N}(a_{y},\,\sigma^{2}_{y}),\qquad a_{y}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{b(y)},\,\nu^{2}_{b(y)}).

The posterior mean is

𝔼⁡[ay∣a~y]=(1−λy)​a~y+λy​μb⁡(y),λy=σy2σy2+νb⁡(y)2.\mathbb{E}[a_{y}\mid\tilde{a}_{y}]=(1-\lambda_{y})\,\tilde{a}_{y}+\lambda_{y}\,\mu_{b(y)},\qquad\lambda_{y}=\frac{\sigma^{2}_{y}}{\sigma^{2}_{y}+\nu^{2}_{b(y)}}. (22)

The more uncertain the class-specific estimate a~y\tilde{a}_{y} is (large σy2\sigma^{2}_{y}), the more it is pulled toward the group mean μb⁡(y)\mu_{b(y)}. For classes with many covered examples, σy2\sigma^{2}_{y} is small and the estimate stays close to the raw value; for rare classes with few examples, the estimate is regularized toward the group prior.

Appendix D Method Details

D.1 Algorithm pseudocode

D.2 Pairwise feature definitions

Table 3 gives the per-dataset pairwise feature specifications.

The score gap directly encodes the base-score threshold t⁡(x,y,j)=gj​(x)−gy​(x)t(x;\,y,j)=g_{j}(x)-g_{y}(x) from Theorem 4.3, allowing the pairwise correction to adapt to the current margin. The domain similarity feature captures how confusable two classes are independent of the current input: taxonomic distance in the biological hierarchy for iNaturalist, WordNet path similarity for ImageNet-LT, and HPO phenotype Jaccard similarity for the rare-disease benchmarks. Places-LT uses four features (no domain similarity available for scene categories).

D.3 Implementation details

Optimization.

All reranker parameters are estimated using L-BFGS-B (scipy.optimize.minimize, maxiter=200–300, ftol=10−1110^{-11}). Wall-clock time is under 30 seconds per dataset per seed on a single CPU.

Hyperparameters.

Table 4 reports the per-dataset settings. All values were selected by grid search on the calibration set (maximizing Hit@1 among covered examples); the test set was never used for selection.

Hyperparameter search grid.

τ∈{0.0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0}\tau\in\{0.0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\}; λa∈{0.0005,0.001,0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5}\lambda_{a}\in\{0.0005,0.001,0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5\}; λθ∈{5×10−5,10−4,5×10−4,10−3,5×10−3,10−2}\lambda_{\theta}\in\{5{\times}10^{-5},10^{-4},5{\times}10^{-4},10^{-3},5{\times}10^{-3},10^{-2}\}; α∈{0.0,0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}\alpha\in\{0.0,0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\}.

Base models.

For iNaturalist, we fine-tune a ResNet-50 (torchvision IMAGENET1K_V2) on the iNat 2018 training split. For ImageNet-LT, we use the publicly available ERM ResNet-50 checkpoint from Kang et al. (2020).11 1 https://github.com/facebookresearch/classifier-balancing For Places-LT, we extract frozen ResNet-152 features (ImageNet-pretrained) and train a logistic-regression classifier with class-balanced weighting (cRT). For GMDB,22 2 https://db.gestaltmatcher.org we select the 508 diseases (out of 528) that have facial phenotype HPO annotations and fine-tune Qwen3.5-0.8B,33 3 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B a multimodal vision-language model, as a 508-way classifier on 7,844 facial images; base logits are pre-normalized by classifier weight norms (gy←gy/‖wy‖0.5g_{y}\leftarrow g_{y}/\|w_{y}\|^{0.5}) before reranking. For RareBench,44 4 https://github.com/chenxz1111/RareBench the same GMDB-trained checkpoint is evaluated in a text-only setting: HPO phenotype terms are formatted as a clinical prompt with a blank 224×\times224 image placeholder, bypassing the visual modality entirely.

Appendix E Datasets and Evaluation

E.1 Dataset details

For ImageNet-LT, we use the ERM ResNet-50 checkpoint from Kang et al. (2020) and split the 50,000-image ILSVRC 2012 validation set into 20,000 calibration and 30,000 test images (seed=42). For Places-LT, we extract frozen ResNet-152 features and retrain a logistic-regression classifier with class-balanced weighting (cRT); the Places365 balanced validation set (∼100{\sim}100 images per class, 18,250 total) is split 60/40 into calibration and test (stratified, seed=42). For RareBench, the GMDB-trained Qwen3.5-0.8B checkpoint is applied out-of-distribution to text-only clinical phenotype descriptions: HPO terms are formatted as a clinical prompt with a blank image placeholder, and the model outputs 508-dim logits over the GMDB disease label space. Of 1,122 RareBench cases, 195 map to 67 GMDB diseases; the remaining cases involve diseases outside the GMDB label set. The rare/frequent split for RareBench follows the GMDB training frequencies over the shared 508-class label space.

Figure 4 shows the training-set class frequency distribution for each benchmark, with the 80/20 rare/frequent boundary marked.

E.2 Evaluation metrics

Hit@kk.

Hit​@​k​(y^)=P⁡(rankr​(Y,X,S⁡(X))≤k∣C)\mathrm{Hit@}k(\hat{y})=P(\mathrm{rank}_{r}(Y,X,S(X))\leq k\mid C). Hit@1 is coverage-conditioned top-1 accuracy within the reranked shortlist. Rare Hit@1 and Frequent Hit@1 apply the same definition after restricting to the corresponding class subsets.

Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR).

MRR⁡(y^)=𝔼⁡[rankr​(Y,X,S⁡(X))−1∣C]\mathrm{MRR}(\hat{y})=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{rank}_{r}(Y,X,S(X))^{-1}\mid C], where rankr\mathrm{rank}_{r} is the position of the true label in the reranked shortlist.

Recall@kk.

Recall​@​k=P⁡(Y∈S⁡(X))\mathrm{Recall@}k=P(Y\in S(X)), the shortlist coverage. This is a property of the base model, not the reranker, and serves as the attainable ceiling for all reranking methods.

Recoverable gap closure (Eq. 9).

ρk=1\rho_{k}=1 means the reranker closes the entire recoverable gap; ρk=0\rho_{k}=0 means no improvement.

Hardest-rival flip rate (Definition 6.1).

Conditions on examples where the base model errs, so the metric is not inflated by examples already handled correctly.

Appendix F Additional Experiments

F.1 Synthetic experiment details

Data generation.

We simulate K=100K=100 classes with a Zipf prior πy∝1/y\pi_{y}\propto 1/y, generating ntrain=5,000n_{\mathrm{train}}=5{,}000 training and ntest=2,000n_{\mathrm{test}}=2{,}000 test examples. Each class yy has a fixed mean μy∼𝒩⁡(0,0.5​I)\mu_{y}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.5I) in ℝ10\mathbb{R}^{10}. For each example, we sample Y∼Categorical⁡(π)Y\sim\mathrm{Categorical}(\pi) and x∼𝒩⁡(μY,I)x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{Y},I). The base model score is gy​(x)=log⁡p⁡(y∣x)+by+ϵg_{y}(x)=\log p(y\mid x)+b_{y}+\epsilon, where by=−τlogπy⋅cb_{y}=-\tau\log\pi_{y}\cdot c is a class-level bias with corruption factor cc, and ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,0.09)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.09). The shortlist is S⁡(x)S(x) = top-10 classes by g⁡(x)g(x).

Class-separable regime.

We set c=0.1c=0.1, introducing a strong class-level bias without any context-dependent confusion. The residual βy⋆​(x,S)\beta^{\star}_{y}(x,S) is approximately constant per class up to a shortlist-shared constant.

Non-class-separable regime with contradictory pairs.

We select 15 confuser pairs (u,v)(u,v) where uu is a tail class and vv is a head class. For each example where both uu and vv appear in the shortlist, we perturb the base scores: gu​(x)+=s⋅δg_{u}(x)\mathrel{+}=s\cdot\delta and gv​(x)-=s⋅δg_{v}(x)\mathrel{-}=s\cdot\delta, where s∼Uniform​{−1,+1}s\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\{-1,+1\} is a per-example context sign and δ=3.0\delta=3.0 is the confusion strength. This creates contradictory threshold requirements across contexts: t⁡(x,u,v)t(x;\,u,v) can be large positive in one context and large negative in another, which is exactly the condition of Theorem 4.3.

Fitting.

The pairwise feature vector ϕ⁡(x,y,j)\phi(x,y,j) consists of three features: the base score gap gy​(x)−gj​(x)g_{y}(x)-g_{j}(x), the rank gap, and the cosine similarity cos⁡(μy,μj)\cos(\mu_{y},\mu_{j}). We maximize the conditional log-likelihood (13) using L-BFGS with λθ=λa=0.001\lambda_{\theta}=\lambda_{a}=0.001. All methods share the same shortlist; only covered examples (yi∈Siy_{i}\in S_{i}) are used for fitting. Results are averaged over 5 seeds.

F.2 Shrinkage diagnostic

For rare classes with only a handful of covered calibration examples, the unshrunk classwise estimate can have high variance. Figure 5 illustrates the intended behavior of the empirical-Bayes shrinkage in a controlled diagnostic: as calibration examples per class increase, the variance gap between the MLE offsets and the shrunk offsets narrows, while the tail-accuracy benefit of shrinkage is largest in the lowest-data regime.

F.3 Component ablation

Figure 6 shows the synthetic ablation in both regimes. Figure 7 extends the analysis to all five real datasets.

F.4 Real-data quintile analysis

Figure 8 shows the gain of REPAIR over Classwise stratified by mean per-class threshold dispersion DyD_{y} on the four real datasets.

RareBench is omitted because its small number of covered classes yields fewer than 15 classes per quintile, making the stratified analysis unreliable.

F.5 Sensitivity to shortlist size

Table 6 evaluates REPAIR across shortlist sizes k∈{5,10,20,50}k\in\{5,10,20,50\}. REPAIR consistently outperforms all baselines at every kk on every dataset. As kk increases, coverage improves but the reranking task becomes harder; the relative advantage of REPAIR over Classwise is stable or grows with kk.

F.6 Unconditional results

Table 7 reports unconditional Hit@1, which factors in coverage: unconditional Hit@1 = conditional Hit@1 ×\times Recall@kk / 100. Since all methods share the same shortlist, unconditional differences mirror the conditional ones.

F.7 Sign test results

Table 8 reports the sign test results for REPAIR vs. Classwise across all dataset–metric pairs. Each cell shows the number of trials (out of 5) in which REPAIR strictly outperforms Classwise.

REPAIR significantly outperforms Classwise on Hit@1, Hit@3, MRR, and Rare Hit@1 across all five datasets (20/20 pass at ≥\geq4/5). HFR passes on four of five datasets; RareBench (3/5) is limited by its small covered test set (32 examples). Frequent Hit@1 passes only on RareBench, where pairwise competition benefits both strata; on the remaining datasets the pairwise term introduces slight noise on frequent classes, as discussed in §6.2.

F.8 RareBench bootstrap confidence intervals

Because RareBench has only 32 covered test examples, we report bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples) to assess the reliability of the observed gains.

The probability that REPAIR outperforms Classwise under resampling is P=0.999P=0.999. On rare classes specifically, the gap is +27.1%+27.1\% with 95%95\% CI [+11.8,+52.9][+11.8,+52.9] (P=0.998P=0.998). Despite the small sample size, the improvement is statistically robust.

Appendix G Limitations

Domain-specific features.

The pairwise feature vector includes a domain-specific similarity component (taxonomic distance, WordNet similarity, or HPO Jaccard) on four of five datasets. When such structured knowledge is unavailable, as on Places-LT, we fall back to a four-dimensional feature vector without domain similarity and still observe gains. A natural alternative in the absence of external knowledge is cosine similarity between the base model’s class embeddings, which we leave for future work.

Shortlist coverage ceiling.

REPAIR operates on a fixed top-kk shortlist produced by the base model and cannot recover examples where the true label falls outside the shortlist. This is a fundamental constraint shared by all post-hoc rerankers, not specific to our method. Our framework explicitly conditions on coverage (Y∈SY\in S) and focuses on maximizing ranking quality within this recoverable set. Improving coverage itself requires modifying the base model, which is orthogonal to the reranking problem we study.
